confidence_note: Law of Solid Ground (trust is the foundation of leadership) and Maxwell's Skyline case come from secondary summaries; the exact details of his three decisions are as reported there. The old text's building-collapse metaphor, quote and 'history examples' were not found and dropped. Vietnam example kept to one short clause.
facts: Law 6, the Law of Solid Ground: trust is the foundation of leadership.
'Character makes trust possible. And trust makes leadership possible.' Leaders cannot lose trust and continue to influence others.
Maxwell compares trust to change in your pocket: good decisions add coins, mistakes take coins out.
He had been senior pastor at Skyline Church for eight years and led it successfully.
He then made three major decisions without his usual process: firing someone, cancelling a service, changing part of the Christmas show.
Trust fell. He apologised publicly and asked forgiveness, and won the congregation's trust back.
Mistakes of ability are easier to recover from than mistakes of character, such as lying about a project's status.
Followers' trust shows in how much they tell you, bad news included.
scene_details: change in a pocket: coins added by good decisions and taken out by mistakes
three decisions: a firing, a cancelled service, a changed Christmas show
a public apology to the congregation
tension: A leader with eight years of credit spends it in three decisions made without his usual process.
opening_idea: Open on the eight years at Skyline and the three decisions made differently.

lessons.idea: When you skip your usual way of deciding, you draw on trust without noticing; a plain apology puts some back.
lessons.anchor: Maxwell's three decisions and the public apology.

reflect_final: Which recent decision of yours skipped the way people expect you to decide, and what would you say to the people it affected?

use_cases.situation: You changed a plan without telling the people who depend on it
use_cases.move: Say: I changed this without checking with you, and that was the wrong way to do it. Here is what I will do next time.

use_cases.situation: A friend broke a promise to you and is avoiding the subject
use_cases.move: Say: Maxwell compares trust to pocket change. I'd like to put a few coins back. Can we talk about what happened?

use_cases.situation: You notice your team only tells you good news
use_cases.move: Ask: what is one thing you hesitated to tell me this week? Thank the answer before reacting.

pocket_idea: Trust works like pocket change: each decision adds or removes coins, and an honest apology can put some back.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Maxwell had led his church well for eight years, and three decisions made outside his usual process still cost him the congregation's trust.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Senior pastor with eight good years makes three big decisions his usual way aside, trust drops, he apologises publicly and wins it back; Maxwell calls trust the foundation of leadership.
